headline: High: CrewAI’s broad filesystem/browser/tool access can amplify Firecrawl outputs into prompt injection, leakage, and unsafe downstream actions by default.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: CrewAI can read/write the host working directory and parse tool outputs in a shared-memory crew, while Firecrawl exposes scraped web content via API/MCP-compatible client support. That creates a plausible default bridge where attacker-controlled web content can reach CrewAI prompts. The interaction is inferred, not directly sandboxed, so uncertainty is resolved upward.
conditions: IF CrewAI ingests Firecrawl-scraped pages or markdown as instructions without provenance filtering, prompt injection is possible.
IF the two agents share a filesystem or message queue, attacker-controlled content can bridge from Firecrawl to CrewAI.
mitigations: Add a strict content-to-instruction separator in the orchestrator.
Strip or neutralize HTML/markdown before CrewAI reads Firecrawl output.
Use a provenance tag and reject untrusted tool output as instructions.
Run both agents in isolated workspaces.
requires-engineering: add allowlisted prompt templates for any Firecrawl-fed task.

B_data_leakage.rationale: CrewAI handles developer-passed crew data, API keys, and broad filesystem access; Firecrawl touches web content, screenshots, structured data, and API keys, with broad network egress. If they share a workspace or credentials, sensitive inputs can flow between them and out to third-party APIs. The pairwise leakage path is plausible from profiles alone, so I rate it medium.
conditions: IF both agents share the same working directory, files containing secrets or scraped data can be read by the other agent.
IF CrewAI forwards Firecrawl outputs into model-provider calls, those contents may leave the local environment.
mitigations: Separate credentials per agent.
Mount distinct working directories.
Disable passing secrets through shared files.
Review outbound API destinations for both agents.
requires-engineering: add DLP/redaction before any model-provider call.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: CrewAI has write_filesystem, execute_shell, subprocesses, and browser execution; Firecrawl has broad network egress and API/CLI client behavior. Even without explicit git overlap, both can mutate shared local artifacts or shared remote resources if orchestrated together. Because shared-state details are developer-defined and not locked by default, conflict risk exists in default pair deployments.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same directory, file clobbering or inconsistent state can occur.
IF the orchestrator routes both agents to the same remote resource without locking, concurrent mutation conflicts can occur.
mitigations: Assign separate output directories.
Serialize writes through one coordinator.
Use file locks for shared artifacts.
Disable browser automation unless needed.
requires-engineering: add optimistic concurrency checks for shared resources.

D_cascading_error.rationale: CrewAI is a multi-agent orchestration framework that can act on tool outputs, while Firecrawl is a crawler/search/extraction agent whose outputs are likely to be treated as facts. If CrewAI consumes Firecrawl results without verification, bad or manipulated web data can cascade into downstream actions. The default blast radius can include irreversible external actions, so high is warranted.
conditions: IF CrewAI uses Firecrawl output as authoritative input, downstream actions may be based on unverified facts.
IF CrewAI is configured to send emails, place orders, or modify records from Firecrawl-derived data, errors can become irreversible.
mitigations: Require a human review step before any external action.
Cross-check Firecrawl results against a second source.
Mark Firecrawl output as untrusted in prompts.
Log source URLs alongside extracted claims.
requires-engineering: add schema validation and confidence thresholds before action execution.

E_compliance.rationale: CrewAI explicitly handles developer-passed crew data and API keys, while Firecrawl touches web content, screenshots, structured data, and API keys. The profiles do not specify residency or certifications, but the combination can move sensitive web-derived data into model-provider and tool integrations. Because compliance details are missing, uncertainty escalates to medium rather than low.
conditions: IF EU personal data is scraped by Firecrawl and then sent through CrewAI to a non-EU processor, residency risk exists.
IF either agent logs retained prompts or screenshots containing regulated data, retention mismatch may occur.
mitigations: Classify data before routing it between agents.
Disable retention of prompts and screenshots where possible.
Use region-appropriate endpoints.
Review vendor DPAs and subprocessors.
requires-engineering: enforce residency-aware routing and retention controls.
